8377.t: From Proto-Hellenic *(s)tégos, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tégos, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teg- (“to cover”). Cognate with Latin tego (“to cover”), German Decke (“roof”), English thatch.

8321.t: From σοφίζω (sophízō, “to become wise”) + -ιστής (-istḗs), from σοφός (sophós, “wise”).

8338.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *stegʷʰ- Proto-Indo-European *-eti Proto-Indo-European *stégʷʰeti Proto-Hellenic *stékʷʰō Ancient Greek στέφω From Proto-Hellenic *stékʷʰō, from Proto-Indo-European *stégʷʰ-e-ti, from *stegʷʰ- (“to enlace”).

8334.t: Adjectival formation from σπάνις (spánis, “rarity, scarcity”). Related to σπανός (spănós, “rare, with scant beard growth”).

8343.t: From στέγω (stégō, “to cover”) + -νός (-nós), with sense development "covered" > "waterproof, clogged".

8378.t: From Proto-Indo-European *(s)teg- (“to cover, roof”). Cognate with Lithuanian sti̇́egiu (“to thatch, to cover a roof”), Latin tegō (“to cover”), Proto-Germanic *þakjaną (“to cover”).

8368.t: From στρέφω (stréphō, “to twist”) and the suffix -μα (-ma).

8380.t: From Proto-Indo-European *sterg- (literally “to cover, to protect”). Possibly related to Proto-Slavic *sterťi (“to guard”) and Welsh serch (“love, affection”).

8336.t: From Proto-Indo-European *stér(h₃)-no-m, from Proto-Indo-European *sterh₃- (“to be broad, spread out”). Cognate with Proto-West Germanic *stirniju (“forehead”).

8316.t: Neumann compares this word with Hittite [script needed] (išḫuwai-, “to throw, scatter, pour”), and Furnée with κύπελλον (kúpellon, “whatever dough and bread is left over on the table”).

8374.t: There are no known cognates. Furnée compares the word with τοπεῖον (topeîon, “rope”).

8370.t: Ultimately from στρέφω (stréphō, “to turn; to rotate”).

8312.t: From Proto-Hellenic *skə́l͏̌l͏̌ō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to split, separate”).

8311.t: According to Beekes, an unexplained formation that must be recent in the prehistory of Greek. The root may be that of σκέπτομαι (sképtomai, “to look about”) or σκάπτω (skáptō, “to dig”), but neither is immediately obvious.

8313.t: The entry by Beekes in his Etymological Dictionary of Greek reads (in paraphrase): :"The basis of this verb is either σκαπ- (skap-) or σκαφ- (skaph-).

8379.t: The entry by Beekes in his Etymological Dictionary of Greek reads: “A full-grade variant of σταφυλή (staphulḗ, “grape”). No further etymology; perhaps Pre-Greek, if the -μ- is interpreted as prenasalization.

8367.t: From the o-grade of στρέφω (stréphō, “to twist, turn”) + -ος (-os).

8335.t: Of disputed origin: * Frisk takes the word as a derivative in -νι- of σπάω (spáō, “to draw, pluck”). * Furnee connects Homeric terms such as ἠπανᾷ (ēpanāî), -νεῖ (-neî)· ἀπορεῖ (aporeî), σπανίζει (spanízei), ἀμηχανεῖ (amēkhaneî, “is without resource”),…

8325.t: Of unclear origin, though the word's ending -άλη (-ắlē) and semantics are reminiscent of those of κραιπάλη (kraipắlē, “bout of drinking”), δαιταλεύς (daităleús, “banqueter”).

8340.t: From the same root as synonymous στάζω (stázō).
